##Data

```{r}
getwd()
file.exists("ps2_script_Ryan.R")
file.exists("data/unemp_raw.rds")

library(tidyquant)
library(tidyverse)

unemp_raw <- tq_get(
  c("UNRATE", "ORUR", "CAUR", "TXUR", "NYUR"),
  get = "economic.data",
  from = "1976-01-01"
)

head(unemp_raw)

dir.create("data", showWarnings = FALSE)

write_rds(unemp_raw, "data/unemp_raw.rds")

unemp_raw = read_rds("data/unemp_raw.rds")


```

##Wrangling

Tables are unemployment rates by region, recent unemployment trneds and the largest unemployment increases and decrease, not counting COVID.

### Unemployment Rate by Region


kable(unemp_summary, digits = 2,
       caption = "Mean unemployment rate by region.")


### Recent Unemployment Summary


kable(unemp_recent_summary, digits = 2,
       caption = "Summary of recent unemployment rates.")


### Five Largest Unemployment Increases (Excluding COVID)


kable(unemp_top_increases_no_covid, digits = 2,
     caption = "Largest increases in unemployment, excluding 2020.")


### Five Largest Unemployment Decreases (Excluding COVID)

###Visualization

###Plot 1: This shows a line graph of the unemployment rate from 1975 to 2026 in every region. The rates go up during major recessions like 2008 and 2020.


ggplot(data = unemp, aes(x = date, y = unemployment_rate, color = region)) +
geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
labs(
 title = "Unemployment Rate Over Time",
x = "Date", y = "Unemployment Rate (%)",  color = "Region") +
  theme_minimal()


###Plot 2: This is a similar graph to the first one except it separates the rates by region.


ggplot(data = unemp, aes(x = date, y = unemployment_rate, color = region)) + geom_line(linewidth = 1) + labs( title = "Unemployment Rate Over Time", x = "Date", y = "Unemployment Rate (%)", color = "Region" ) + theme_minimal() + facet_wrap(~ region)


###Plot 3: This is a bar graph of the average unemployment reate in percentage by region. California and Oregon have the highest average rates.

ggplot(data = unemp_summary, aes(x = fct_reorder(region, mean_rate), y = mean_rate)) + geom_col() + labs( title = "Average Unemployment Rate by Region", x = "Region", y = "Average Unemployment Rate (%)" ) + theme_minimal()


###Plot 4: This was a boxplot ofmy own creation that shows the median, 25 and 75 quartiles and any outliers of unemployment rate by region.

ggplot(unemp, aes(x = region, y = unemployment_rate)) + geom_boxplot() + labs( title = "Unemployment Rate Distribution by Region", x = "Region", y = "Unemployment Rate (%)" ) + coord_flip()

###Reflection I found this second project both easier and harder than I initially anticipated. The actual lines of code I found quite easy, especially due to the starter code provided which I thought was a very good way to ease into it. What I found difficult was publishing my results to Github and figuring out the Quarto document, so basically everything that is not involved with R itself. I feel much more comfortable with graphing into ggplot2 as well and found the customization infteresting. I now feel more confident with basic data composition and mutation. ---

## Quarto

Quarto enables you to weave together content and executable code into a finished document. To learn more about Quarto see <https://quarto.org>.

## Running Code

When you click the **Render** button a document will be generated that includes both content and the output of embedded code. You can embed code like this:

```{r}
1 + 1
```

You can add options to executable code like this

```{r}
#| echo: false
2 * 2
```

The `echo: false` option disables the printing of code (only output is displayed).
